title: HNSW I: small-world graphs, the intuition
summary: Greedy search on a pure nearest-neighbour graph gets 1.3 percent recall and stops after 1.7 hops, because every edge is short and local minima are everywhere. Eight random long edges per node more than double it, and HNSW is a skip list for metric space built on that idea.
html:
Yesterday's IVF divides space into cells and scans whole cells. Today's idea is different: build a graph over the vectors and walk it. Follow edges toward the query and stop when you cannot get closer.

The appeal is obvious. A walk touches the nodes it passes and nothing else, so cost depends on path length rather than corpus size. The catch is that the obvious graph does not work, and finding out exactly how it fails is the fastest route to understanding why HNSW is built the way it is.

Greedy search on a proximity graph

Connect every vector to its M nearest neighbours. To search:

current = some entry point
loop:
    look at current's neighbours
    if one is closer to the query than current: move there
    else: stop, current is the answer

Hill climbing. About eight lines. I ran it on the 6,200 real document embeddings from yesterday, 300 held-out queries, entry point chosen at random, measuring how often it lands on the true nearest neighbour:

pure proximity graph, M=4    recall@1  0.013   avg hops  1.7
pure proximity graph, M=8    recall@1  0.047   avg hops  2.3
pure proximity graph, M=16   recall@1  0.163   avg hops  2.8
pure proximity graph, M=32   recall@1  0.320   avg hops  2.8

One point three percent at M=4. The graph is built from true nearest neighbours and greedy search finds the right answer essentially never.

Read the hop count, not the recall

The recall column tells you it failed. The hop column tells you why, and it is the more interesting number.

Average 1.7 hops. The search is not wandering the graph and ending up somewhere wrong. It takes one or two steps and stops, because every neighbour of where it stands is further from the query than it is. That is a local minimum, and on a pure proximity graph they are everywhere.

The reason is structural. If every edge goes to a near neighbour, every edge is short. Your entry point lands in some arbitrary region, and there is no edge that crosses the space. You are in a village where every road leads to the next house, trying to reach another county.

Raising M helps a little, and it helps for a boring reason: more neighbours means more chances one of them is closer, so you escape shallow minima. It does not add any long edges, and doubling M doubles your memory. M=32 gets to 0.320 and that is not a path to 0.95.

Small worlds

Watts and Strogatz published the fix in 1998, for a different problem. Take a regular lattice where everything connects to its immediate neighbours. Path lengths are terrible, O(N). Now rewire a small fraction of edges to random distant nodes. Clustering barely changes, and the average path length collapses toward O(log N).

That is a small-world network, and it is the formal version of six degrees of separation. Most of your friends live near you, a few do not, and those few are what make the whole world reachable in a handful of steps.

Applied here: keep the proximity edges for precision near the target, add a few long edges for reachability. I added purely random edges to the M=16 graph:

M=16 alone                          recall@1  0.163
M=16 plus 1 random long edge        recall@1  0.227
M=16 plus 2 random long edges       recall@1  0.237
M=16 plus 4 random long edges       recall@1  0.293
M=16 plus 8 random long edges       recall@1  0.340

Eight random edges per node more than doubles recall, and matches what M=32 achieved using twice the edges of the useful kind. Randomly chosen, carrying no information about the data, worth more than doubling the careful ones. That is the small-world effect, measured.

Where the hierarchy comes in

NSW, the predecessor to HNSW, gets these long edges for free through a trick worth appreciating. Build the graph by inserting vectors one at a time, connecting each new one to the nearest neighbours findable in the graph so far. Early insertions happen when the graph is sparse and their links are necessarily long-range. Later ones are short. The long edges are a fossil of insertion order.

HNSW makes it explicit instead of incidental. Assign each node a maximum layer from an exponentially decaying distribution, so layer 0 holds everything, layer 1 holds a fraction, and the top holds a handful. Search starts at the top, greedily descends, and drops a layer whenever it stops improving.

If you have implemented a skip list, you already know this structure. Same probabilistic layering, same coarse-to-fine descent, same expected O(log N). HNSW is a skip list for metric space, and the sparse top layers do exactly what the express lanes do: get you near the right region in a few long hops so the dense bottom layer only has to do local work.

The measurable part of that is the entry point. Instead of starting at random, start somewhere already close:

M=16, random entry point              recall@1  0.163
M=16, best of 16 random candidates    recall@1  0.300

Doubling again, purely from starting in a better place. That is all the upper layers are for.

One more thing the real algorithm does

My graphs connect each node to its M nearest neighbours, which sounds obviously right and is not. If a node sits at the edge of a cluster, its 16 nearest neighbours are all back inside that cluster, pointing the same way. Sixteen edges, one direction, fifteen of them redundant.

HNSW instead uses a selection heuristic: consider candidates nearest first, and keep one only if it is closer to the node being connected than to any neighbour already chosen. A candidate sitting behind an existing edge gets dropped. What survives is a set of edges spread across different directions, which is what makes a walk able to leave in the first place.

So the long edges from the small-world argument and the diverse edges from the pruning heuristic are solving the same problem from two sides: a graph where every edge points into the same neighbourhood is a graph you cannot navigate.

What is still missing

Long edges and a good entry point together get to roughly 0.34. HNSW does 0.95 and better. So something structural is still absent, and it is not the graph.

It is the search. Everything above tracks a single current node, which is why one bad step ends the walk. Real HNSW keeps a candidate list of size ef and expands the most promising unvisited node each round, so a dead end costs one candidate rather than the query. On the same M=16 graph with the same random entry points, going from a single pointer to a list of 64 moves recall from 0.163 to 0.947.

That parameter, and the two that go with it, are tomorrow: M, efConstruction and efSearch, what each one actually buys, and which of them you are allowed to change after the index is built.
exercise:
1. Build the graph and watch it get stuck. Take any embeddings, compute the M nearest neighbours of every vector with one argpartition over the similarity matrix, and write the eight line greedy walk. Print the hop count alongside the recall. Seeing it terminate after two hops is the thing worth seeing.

2. Add random edges and re-measure. Append a few uniformly random node ids to each adjacency list and rerun. You should get a jump comparable to doubling M, from edges that cost you nothing to compute. If you do not, check that your entry points are genuinely random, because starting near the answer hides the whole effect.

3. Find the skip list. Write down, in two sentences, what corresponds to what: skip list levels and HNSW layers, the express lane and the long edge, the level coin flip and the layer distribution. If that mapping is solid, tomorrow's parameters will feel like tuning a structure you already know rather than memorising three new names.
